questions.text: A rectangular beam is 60 mm × 280 mm (actual dimensions). Applied shear V = 20 kN. Allowable shear stress Fv = 1.3 MPa. Calculate applied shear stress fv and determine compliance.

options.text: fv = 1.786 MPa > Fv = 1.3 MPa. The member FAILS the shear check.
fv = 0.893 MPa < Fv = 1.3 MPa. The member PASSES the shear check.
fv = 1.19 MPa < Fv = 1.3 MPa. The member PASSES the shear check.
fv = 3.57 MPa > Fv = 1.3 MPa. The member FAILS the shear check.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: fv = V/A (no 3/2 factor) = 20,000 / 16,800 = 1.19 MPa. This is the average shear, not the maximum; the 3/2 factor is mandatory.
rationale.d: This is 0.5 × 1.786 MPa (missing the 3/2 factor entirely or dividing by 2 instead of multiplying).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A timber beam must satisfy both bending and shear checks. The bending check yields fb = 9 MPa (Fb = 12 MPa, OK), and the shear check yields fv = 1.6 MPa (Fv = 1.2 MPa, FAIL). What is the controlling factor, and what design change is most efficient?

options.text: Shear is controlling. Increase width (b) or height (h) to reduce fv = 3V/(2bh). Height is less efficient than width for shear.
Bending is controlling. Increase depth (h) to increase S = bh²/6 and reduce fb, ensuring the beam can handle greater loads
Both checks fail equally; increase both strength and stiffness simultaneously, which may involve using a different material or cross-section
Shear failure is less critical; proceed with the current design and monitor in service, accepting the risk of potential failure

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Bending passes; it is not the controlling check. Increasing h (depth) _increases_ S and reduces fb, which has already passed.
rationale.d: Both do not fail. The check that fails is the one that governs the design.
rationale.correct: Shear fails (1.6 > 1.2); bending passes (9 < 12). Shear is the governing (limiting) check. To reduce fv, increase A = bh. Since fv is inversely proportional to h (in the denominator), increasing height helps, but _width_ has equal effect on A and is mechanically simpler to increase without affecting bending adversely.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 6.2 (Combined Stress Checks); ASEAN TCS 1-2019 Section 6.2

questions.text: A design uses a timber beam with section modulus S = 1,200,000 mm³ and allowable bending stress Fb = 11 MPa. What is the maximum moment the beam can safely carry?

options.text: M_max = 13.2 kN·m
M_max = 132 kN·m
M_max = 1.32 kN·m
M_max = 1,320 kN·m

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: 132 kN·m would require S = 12,000,000 mm³ (ten times larger).
rationale.d: 1.32 kN·m is 1/10 of the correct answer (dimensional error in converting N·mm to kN·m).
rationale.correct: From fb = M/S, rearranging: M = fb × S. At the allowable limit, fb = Fb = 11 MPa = 11 N/mm². M_max = 11 × 1,200,000 = 13,200,000 N·mm = 13.2 kN·m.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: In ASD timber design, the bending stress check is fb ≤ Fb. What does fb represent?

options.text: Applied bending stress, calculated as M/S
Allowable bending stress, looked up from design tables
Fiber allowable stress, always equal to 12 MPa
Buckling factor for lateral instability

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Fb (uppercase) is the allowable stress, not fb.
rationale.d: Fb is 'fiber allowable,' but its value varies by species and grade, not fixed at 12 MPa.
rationale.correct: Lowercase fb = applied bending stress = M/S. It is computed from loads (moment M) and section properties (S). Uppercase Fb = allowable bending stress from tables.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 6.2 (Timber Design - ASD); ASEAN TCS 1-2019 Section 6.2

questions.text: A timber beam experiences an applied moment M = 18 kN·m and has section modulus S = 800,000 mm³. Calculate the applied bending stress fb.

options.text: fb = 22.5 MPa
fb = 0.0225 MPa
fb = 44.4 MPa
fb = 225 MPa

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This results from incorrect unit conversion; 18 kN·m ÷ 800,000 × 10⁻⁹ (wrong power of 10).
rationale.d: This is approximately 18 × 10⁶ / 800,000 / 1000 (extra factor of 1000). Units must be consistent (all N·mm or all kN·m with mm³ adjusted).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A timber beam shows applied bending stress fb = 14 MPa and allowable bending stress Fb = 12 MPa. What design action is required?

options.text: The member fails the bending check (fb > Fb). Increase dimensions, select higher grade, or use stiffer species.
The member passes the check with a safety margin. No action is required, as the current design is sufficient for the applied loads.
Reduce the applied load to make fb equal to Fb, ensuring that the stress does not exceed the allowable limit.
Use the ratio Fb/fb = 0.86 as a strength reduction factor in subsequent calculations, which may affect future design considerations.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: The inequality is NOT satisfied (14 > 12); the member fails, not passes.
rationale.d: Reducing load is not a structural design action; it changes the load case and requires project scope modification.
rationale.correct: fb = 14 MPa exceeds Fb = 12 MPa. The member is undersized and non-compliant. Redesign is mandatory: increase b or h (depth h has greatest effect due to h² term), specify a higher grade, or select a higher-strength species.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: For a rectangular timber section, what is the moment of inertia I used in deflection checks?

options.text: I = bh³/12
I = bh²/6
I = bh²/12
I = b³h/12

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: I = bh²/6 is the section modulus S, not moment of inertia. S is used for stress; I is used for deflection.
rationale.d: I = bh²/12 is dimensionally incorrect for moment of inertia (missing one h).
rationale.correct: I = bh³/12. Moment of inertia is proportional to the _cube_ of the larger dimension (depth h in vertical bending). The 12 is the denominator for rectangular sections.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 6.2.2 (Section Properties); structural mechanics textbooks

questions.text: A timber beam of nominal dimensions 4×10 (actual 89 mm × 240 mm) is designed for bending using Fb = 10 MPa from the design table. During construction, green timber (higher moisture) is delivered, and the engineer must apply a moisture adjustment factor of 0.9. What is the effective allowable bending stress for the green timber, and what design action is required if the applied stress fb = 9.5 MPa?

options.text: Effective Fb = 9.0 MPa. Since fb = 9.5 MPa > 9.0 MPa, the member FAILS under green conditions and must be reinforced or replaced with kiln-dried timber.
Effective Fb = 10 MPa (adjustment factors apply only to strength, not to design); the member remains acceptable, as the design stress is within allowable limits
Effective Fb = 11.1 MPa (adjustment increases allowable); the member improves under green conditions, providing additional safety margin
The moisture adjustment factor only affects compression; bending stresses are unaffected, allowing the member to be used without modification

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Adjustment factors are mandatory and directly applied to allowable stress. Ignoring them is non-compliant.
rationale.d: Green timber has lower strength; the adjustment factor < 1.0, reducing Fb, not increasing it.
rationale.correct: Adjustment factors multiply the tabulated allowable stress. Fb_green = Fb_dry × 0.9 = 10 × 0.9 = 9.0 MPa. Applied fb = 9.5 MPa exceeds the adjusted allowable (9.0 MPa). The member fails under green conditions and cannot be used without redesign or drying.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 6.3.2 (Adjustment Factors - Wet Service); ASEAN TCS 1-2019 Section 5.2

questions.text: Identify the correct formula for horizontal shear stress in a rectangular timber section.

options.text: fv = 3V/(2A), where A = bh
fv = V/A, where A = bh, which is a simplified version often used for quick calculations
fv = 1.5V/A, where A = bh/2, which is incorrect due to the division by 2
fv = V/(bh²), which is a common error in understanding the formula

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: fv = V/A (no 3/2 factor) is the average shear; it underestimates maximum shear by 50%.
rationale.d: This is dimensionally incorrect; bh/2 is not the appropriate area for shear stress.
rationale.correct: fv = 3V/(2A) is the exact formula for rectangular sections. The 3/2 factor accounts for the parabolic shear distribution, with peak shear at the neutral axis.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 6.2.3 (Horizontal Shear); ASEAN TCS 1-2019 Section 6.2

questions.text: A rectangular timber beam is 80 mm wide × 250 mm deep. What is the section modulus S?

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: S = bh/6 (missing h exponent) = 80 × 250 / 6 = 3,333 mm³. This is wrong; the exponent is mandatory.
rationale.d: This is I/r calculation or a dimensional error; it does not match the formula.
rationale.correct: S = bh²/6 = 80 × 250² / 6 = 80 × 62,500 / 6 = 5,000,000 / 6 = 833,333 mm³. The h² (height squared) is critical.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.
